With the growing popularity of vibecoding, the number of new apps hitting the App Store has surged, doubling in the first half of 2026 — yet downloads have grown by just 2%. Here are the details.

Surge in new app submissions fails to translate into download growth

A report published today by The New York Times, citing the latest data from Sensor Tower, shows that the number of new apps submitted to the App Store doubled in the first half of 2026, while downloads grew by only 2%:

The New York Times report also spotlights two developers who have been putting vibecoded apps on the App Store. One is Marco Pérez, who plans to leave his job at JPMorgan next month to develop apps full-time; the other is David Svensson, who has launched 11 niche apps over the past five months, treating vibecoding as a hobby rather than a business opportunity.

Below is an excerpt from the report:

Pérez, a software engineer based in Chicago who had never built a mobile app before, spent five weeks over the winter tinkering with "vibecoding" AI tools to create a prototype, and another two weeks preparing it for the Apple App Store. The app, called InfoDrizzle, has performed modestly, recording around 1,300 downloads and earning roughly $500 in profit. Pérez's next app has fared better. In May, he spent about a week building Stampa — a scrapbooking app that turns photos into digital stamps. Stampa has since been downloaded 20,000 times, earning around $3,000 in profit.

Apple spokesperson Peter Ajemian, responding to The New York Times, addressed another impact of this submission boom: earlier reports suggested that the App Store's review process has come under strain as a result.

Ajemian said Apple "has been able to review 90% of app submissions within 48 hours," adding that Apple is "delighted to see a new generation of developers using the latest tools to build and ship apps faster."

He also stressed that "all apps must meet the same high standards of quality, privacy and safety that users have always relied on," regardless of whether they are built using vibecoding.
